newsitem.title: UK: Britons likely to face referendum on voting reform.
newsitem.headline: Britons likely to face referendum on voting reform.

text.p: Britain's imminent election could be the last to be held under the widely criticised first-past-the-post voting system under plans published on Wednesday by the country's two main opposition parties.

The Labour Party said it had agreed with the Liberal Democrats to hold a referendum on adopting proportional representation (PR) if it wins the election, expected to be held on May 1. Opinion polls make Labour the clear favourite.

The two parties also agreed on detailed plans for sweeping changes to Britain's constitution, ranging from setting up separate parliaments in Scotland and Wales and abolishing the right of hereditary peers to sit in the upper House of Lords, to bringing in Britain's first freedom of information act.
Under the first-past-the-post system, votes are cast in single-member seats and victory goes to the candidate with the highest number of votes.
The Conservatives have won overall majorities in four successive general elections without polling more than 44 percent of the vote in any of them.
The system would give Labour, currently taking nearly 50 percent of the vote in opinion polls, a massive majority in the new parliament.
A change to PR would revolutionise the British political scene, meaning that single-party governments with an overall majority of seats in parliament would become the exception rather than the rule.
"This is an historic occasion," said Labour's Foreign Affairs spokesman Robin Cook, who led his party in four months of talks with the Liberal Democrats.
"Two political parties who will be competing against each other in the general election have cooperated together to agree on a radical and comprehensive programme of constitutional reform."

At the 1992 general election the centrist Liberal Democrats won just 20 seats in the 651-member House of Commons despite polling more than one-sixth of all votes cast. They have long railed at what they see as the injustice of the first-past-the-post system.
The Labour-Liberal document commits the parties to PR voting for the proposed Scottish and Welsh parliaments and for the election of British members of the European Parliament in 1999.
Labour leader Tony Blair has in the past expressed scepticism about PR for the lower House of Commons.

He fears it could make Liberals the kingmakers of British politics, determining which of the two major parties forms a government in the same way as their Free Democrat counterparts often do in Germany.
But Robert Maclennan, President of the Liberal Democrats, said neither party had been the victors in the negotiations.
"These talks have seen no party winners and no party losers. The true gainers will be the people of Britain," he said.
Maclennan denied that the agreement was the fore-runner of cooperation between the two parties in government after the election.
"Our position is a reflection of the new politics but does not presage a wider commitment to dissolve the identities of our two parties, which are distinct, historic and separate," he said.
